docs.title: Welcome to OAAX
docs.text:
OAAX (Open AI Accelerator eXchange) is an open standard that lets one ONNX model run on many AI accelerators through one conversion step and one runtime API. Export your model from any framework to ONNX, convert it with the accelerator's toolchain, and load it from your application through the same C interface on every chip. No framework or vendor specific integration.

OAAX is an open-source, community-driven project of the LF AI & Data Foundation.

docs.title: OAAX Manager: get a runtime or toolchain in one command
docs.text:
What it is for. Every accelerator ships a runtime library and a conversion toolchain, in several builds (CPU architecture, CUDA or HailoRT version, Ubuntu version). oaax-manager finds the right one for your machine, downloads it, checks its checksum and unpacks it, so you never hunt for download links.

How to use it. It needs uv and nothing else; run it without installing anything:

uvx oaax-manager list                       # everything available; * marks builds that fit this OS and CPU
uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime cpu          # downloads and unpacks the runtime for this machine
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain cpu        # saves the toolchain image and prints the `docker load` command

Replace cpu with intel, nvidia-ort, nvidia-trt, hailo or deepx. When a chip has several builds (several CUDA versions, HailoRT versions or Ubuntu versions can all be marked *), it never guesses: it lists them and you choose with --variant.

Command or option What it does list [--kind runtime\|toolchain] [--vendor V] Show the available runtimes and toolchains fetch runtime <vendor> Download, verify and extract the runtime for this OS and CPU fetch toolchain <vendor> Download and verify the toolchain Docker image (.tar) --variant V Pick a build when several exist (for example cuda12, hailort4.20.0) --os, --arch Fetch a runtime for another platform (for example --arch aarch64) --artifact-version X.Y.Z Pin an OAAX version (default: the newest) -o DIR Where to write

Safe by default

Every download is checked against a pinned SHA-256, interrupted downloads resume, archives are extracted all-or-nothing with strict path checks, and an existing folder is never overwritten.

Install it permanently with uv tool install oaax-manager, or download the single file oaax-manager.pyz from the releases page and run it with any Python 3.9+ (python3 oaax-manager.pyz list). Details: PyPI, GitHub.

docs.title: How OAAX works
docs.text:
1. Convert the ONNX model with the accelerator's toolchain. The result is an OAAX bundle for that chip.
  2. Load the accelerator's runtime library in your application, and call runtime_init(config).
  3. Load the model with runtime_load_models(num_models, model_configs). A model is referred to by its index in model_configs (its model_id).
  4. Exchange data asynchronously.
    1. Enqueue inputs with runtime_enqueue_input(model_id, input_tensors), setting a unique id on each Tensors.
    2. Retrieve outputs with runtime_retrieve_output(&model_id, &output_tensors, timeout_ms). The output carries the id of the input it answers.
  5. Clean up with runtime_cleanup().

The application code is the same for every chip: only the runtime library and the model file change. See the specification and the interface header for the full API.

Terminology
  • OAAX: Open AI Accelerator eXchange, a standard (specification, recipe) for deploying AI models across different hardware accelerators.
  • XPU, AI accelerator or AI hardware: Any processing unit that can execute AI models, such as CPUs, GPUs, NPUs or specialized AI accelerators.
  • Compile or Convert: Turning an ONNX model into a format optimized and supported for a specific XPU.
  • Runtime: The shared library (.so or .dll) that implements the OAAX runtime interface to interact with an XPU.
  • Conversion toolchain: The software that compiles ONNX models.
  • Input/Output tensors: Data structures (Tensors) that hold the input and output data for the model.
  • Host or runtime host: The software that uses a runtime to offload model computation to the AI hardware.
  • OAAX-compliant XPU: Any AI accelerator with an implementation of the OAAX standard, both the conversion toolchain and the runtime library.

docs.text: 📦 Implementation details The CPU runtime & toolchain are implemented in the Github repository. Latest release: v2.0.0 (checksums are in its release notes).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The CPU implementation is the baseline OAAX runtime and toolchain. It runs on any supported CPU, needs no driver, and is the quickest way to try OAAX or to start your own accelerator implementation.

  • Toolchain: loads the ONNX model and simplifies it with ONNX Simplifier (checks the graph, folds constants, removes unused nodes; the result is checked against the original on 3 random inputs). It does not quantize, change the precision, rename or reshape the inputs and outputs, or compile for a device. If simplification fails, the original model is kept and the failure is logged.
  • Runtime: loads the .onnx file (or the model bytes from memory) into ONNX Runtime and runs it asynchronously on worker threads.
  • Tensors: the runtime passes your input tensors to ONNX Runtime as they are, using the tensor names declared in the ONNX graph. Data types (float, float16, int8, uint8, ..., float8), batch sizes and dynamic dimensions are whatever the model and ONNX Runtime accept; the runtime does not check them before inference (see bad input).

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Needed to run Needed to convert x86_64 CPU with AVX2 (the library is built with -march=haswell), or an aarch64 CPU. Memory: each model is loaded once per worker replica (see num_replicas). A x86_64 machine that runs Docker. No GPU, no accelerator.

docs.text:
Needed to run Needed to convert Linux: glibc 2.29 or higher (Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 11+), libstdc++6, and on x86_64 libgomp1 (sudo apt-get install libgomp1). The CI tests the runtime on Ubuntu 22.04. Docker on x86_64, and about 1.7 GB of disk (835 MB .tar + 809 MB image). Windows: 10 or 11, x86_64. The Visual C++ runtime DLLs are shipped in the archive. The image bundles Python 3.11, ONNX 1.21.0, ONNX Simplifier 0.4.36 and ONNX Runtime 1.21.1.

Also needed for the end-to-end example

uv runs oaax-manager: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh, then export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH". To build the host on a minimal image: sudo apt-get install -y git curl cmake build-essential libgomp1 ca-certificates.

docs.title: Get the runtime and toolchain
docs.text:
There is a single build per platform (no variants), so no variant needs to be picked.

oaax-managerManual 
uvx oaax-manager list                    # all builds; * marks this machine's runtime
uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime cpu       # writes runtime-cpu-2.0.0-linux-x86_64/libRuntimeLibrary.so
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain cpu     # saves oaax-cpu-toolchain-2.0.0.tar
docker load -i oaax-cpu-toolchain-2.0.0.tar

Use --os linux|windows and --arch x86_64|aarch64 to fetch the runtime of another platform. SHA-256 sums are verified for you.

curl -LO https://nbg1.your-objectstorage.com/oaax/runtimes/2.0.0/CPU/x86_64/Ubuntu/library.tar.gz
echo "f3b71a075b0db7bbc164ca8a3029e719e71a3bcf896ba29232e150ee7a9bc920  library.tar.gz" | sha256sum -c
mkdir cpu-runtime && tar xzf library.tar.gz -C cpu-runtime      # -> cpu-runtime/libRuntimeLibrary.so

The other checksums are in the release notes.

docs.title: Conversion toolchain
docs.text:
The image takes one .onnx file (not a .zip bundle) and an output directory. It has no other option, no config.json and no environment variable.

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/model:/model" oaax-cpu-toolchain:2.0.0 /model/model.onnx /model/output
Argument Meaning <onnx-path> Path inside the container of a file ending in .onnx. <output-directory> Path inside the container; created if missing. --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" The image runs as user 1000 (appuser); without this flag it can only write to directories that user owns. -v "$PWD/model:/model" Mounts the host directory holding the model. It must be writable (not :ro).

The input directory is written to

The toolchain first saves <model-name>-simplified.onnx next to the input file, then copies it to the output directory. Expect one extra file in the directory you mounted.

Output in <output-directory>: <model-name>-simplified.onnx (the model to give to the runtime) and logs.json, an array of {"Message": ..., "Data": {...}} entries:

logs.json entries and fields Message Data fields Simplifying ONNX model ONNX Path, MD5, Size (bytes) Simplified ONNX model successfully Nodes before, Nodes after, Duration (s) Failed to simplify ONNX model (instead of the previous one) Error, Fallback (the original file is used) Successful Conversion (always last) Output Directory, Output file name, MIME type (application/x-onnx; device=cpu), Output file MD5, Output size (bytes), Logs file name

Note

Successful Conversion is also written when simplification failed and the original model was kept: look for Failed to simplify ONNX model in logs.json. If the toolchain stops with an error, no logs.json is written.

Error (exit code) Meaning Usage: ... <onnx-path> <output-directory> (1) Not exactly two arguments. error: File not found: <path> (2) The path does not exist inside the container: check the -v mount. error: --onnx-path must point to a .onnx file (2) Wrong extension, for example a .zip. PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied / Read-only file system (1) Missing --user $(id -u):$(id -g), or a read-only mount. DecodeError: ... Wire format was corrupt (1) The file is not a valid ONNX model.

docs.title: Runtime library
docs.text: Extract libRuntimeLibrary.so (or RuntimeLibrary.dll) and load it from the host application: see the specification and the C example. Config keys and values are strings; unknown keys (including num_threads, which 2.0.0 no longer reads) are ignored.

docs.title: runtime_init keys
docs.text:
Key Values Default Meaning log_level 0 trace, 1 debug, 2 info, 3 warning, 4 error, 5 critical, 6 off 2 Minimal level, for the console and the file. Anything else falls back to 2. log_file path runtime.log Log file, relative to the working directory. perf_mode eco, power eco CPU budget: eco uses 40% and power 90% of the logical cores (at least 1). num_intra_threads integer >= 0 0 (4) ONNX Runtime threads per inference. 0 means 4. num_replicas integer >= 0 0 (derived) Parallel copies of each model, i.e. inferences in flight. 0 means max(1, budget / intra threads).

The thread budget per model is max(1, floor(cores * 0.4 or 0.9) / number of models). On a 20-thread machine, eco gives a budget of 8, so 2 replicas x 4 threads; power gives 18, so 4 replicas x 4 threads. Each replica holds its own copy of the model, so memory grows with num_replicas. Higher throughput needs more replicas; lower latency per request needs more intra threads.

ModelConfig.config is not read: there are no per-model keys. Use file_path, or model_data + model_size to load from memory (if model_size is 0, file_path is used).

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Topic Behavior Logging Written to stdout and to log_file (rotates at 5 MB, keeps 3 files). Every request failure is logged at error level. Models Load all models in one runtime_load_models call; a model's id is its index. A failed load leaves nothing loaded and you may call it again. Concurrency runtime_enqueue_input and runtime_retrieve_output can be called from different threads. All models share one output queue; model_id tells which model answered. Ordering With more than one replica, outputs can arrive in any order: match them to requests with Tensors.id. Limits Each model queues about 1,000 pending requests (measured: the first failure came at about 1,150 with 1 replica); then runtime_enqueue_input returns ERROR (1) with input queue full. runtime_retrieve_output(timeout_ms): negative waits forever, 0 does not wait. Diagnostics runtime_get_info() returns {"loaded_models":N,"requests_in_flight":N,"backend_version":"..."} (queued requests, not those running). Cleanup Always call runtime_cleanup() before exiting or unloading: the process aborts at exit otherwise.

docs.title: Status codes and bad input
docs.text:
Status codes by call Call Status (code) and cause runtime_init ALREADY_INITIALIZED (3) when called twice; INVALID_ARGUMENT (5) for a bad perf_mode, or a non-integer or negative num_intra_threads / num_replicas; ERROR (1) if the log file cannot be opened. runtime_load_models NOT_INITIALIZED (2); ALREADY_INITIALIZED (3) on a second call; INVALID_ARGUMENT (5) for n <= 0; ERROR (1) for every model problem (missing file, invalid ONNX, no path given): read runtime_get_error(). runtime_enqueue_input NOT_INITIALIZED (2), MODEL_NOT_LOADED (4), INVALID_MODEL_ID (18), INVALID_ARGUMENT (5) for a null pointer, ERROR (1) when the model's queue is full. runtime_retrieve_output NO_OUTPUT_AVAILABLE (12) when nothing arrived before the timeout.

Wrong tensors are not rejected

runtime_enqueue_input returns success for a tensor with the wrong name, data type or shape. The inference then fails inside ONNX Runtime, the error is written to the log (for example Unexpected input data type. Actual: (tensor(float16)), expected: (tensor(float))), and no output is ever produced for that request. A host that only sees NO_OUTPUT_AVAILABLE should check the log.

docs.title: End-to-end example
docs.text:
Runs the official YOLOX-S detector (36 MB, 80 COCO classes, no NMS inside) from .onnx to detections with the generic YOLOX example host, which is the same for every chip. Needs Ubuntu 22.04+ on x86_64, Docker and the tools above. It downloads about 880 MB (835 MB toolchain, 36 MB model, 8.5 MB runtime) and uses 809 MB more for the Docker image. Run in a clean Ubuntu 22.04 container, the whole sequence took 35 s on a fast connection.

  1. Build the host and fetch the model (checked against a pinned sha256):

    git clone https://github.com/OAAX-standard/examples.git
cd examples/yolox-example
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build
bash fetch_model.sh                          # writes models/yolox_s.onnx

  2. Download the runtime and the toolchain, and load the toolchain image:

    uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime cpu
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain cpu
docker load -i oaax-cpu-toolchain-2.0.0.tar      # prints: Loaded image: oaax-cpu-toolchain:2.0.0

  3. Convert the model (about 2 s of simplification):

    mkdir -p model && cp models/yolox_s.onnx model/
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/model:/model" oaax-cpu-toolchain:2.0.0 /model/yolox_s.onnx /model/output
ls model/output      # logs.json  yolox_s-simplified.onnx

  4. Run inference:

    ./build/yolox_host runtime-cpu-2.0.0-linux-x86_64/libRuntimeLibrary.so model/output/yolox_s-simplified.onnx artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg

Expected output (timings depend on your CPU; here a 20-thread machine in use):

Runtime: OAAX CPU Runtime 2.0.0
Runtime info: {"loaded_models":1,"requests_in_flight":0,"backend_version":"1.17.3"}
Input: 'images' float32 NCHW, 1280x854 image letterboxed to 640
Output tensor 'output': type 1, shape [1, 8400, 85]
Detections (score >= 0.30, NMS IoU 0.45): 2
  bicycle        0.953  ( 616,  210) - (1228,  806)
  dog            0.934  ( 216,  244) - ( 521,  587)
Wrote detections.png
OK: 10 requests, first 93.9 ms (warm-up), then 104.5 ms on average (min 89.0 ms)

detections.png is the picture shown on the Hello World page. Simplification only removed 4 of the 279 nodes (the CPU runtime also runs the unconverted model). Pass options of the table above to the host with --config KEY=VALUE, for example --config perf_mode=power. The Windows and aarch64 runtimes were not run for this page (not verified on hardware).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix Permission denied: '/model/...' when converting Run the container as yourself: --user $(id -u):$(id -g), and do not mount the model directory read-only. File not found: /model/... The path is read inside the container; it must start with the mount target (/model). must point to a .onnx file The CPU toolchain takes the .onnx itself, not a .zip. DecodeError, or an empty output file after converting an empty .onnx The input is not a valid ONNX model. Re-export it. An empty file is "converted" to an empty file, and the runtime then fails to load it (ModelProto does not have a graph). runtime_init returns 5 See runtime_get_error(): perf_mode must be "eco" or "power", or num_intra_threads and num_replicas must be .... runtime_init returns 1 with Logger initialization failed The folder of log_file does not exist or is not writable. runtime_load_models returns 1 Read runtime_get_error(): File doesn't exist, ModelProto does not have a graph, or file_path and model_data are both null. Requests succeed but no output arrives Check the log for Inference error for request N: a wrong tensor name (Invalid input name), data type (Unexpected input data type, for example float16 sent to a float32 model) or shape (Got invalid dimensions). libgomp.so.1: cannot open shared object file or GLIBC_2.29 not found Install libgomp1; the OS is older than Ubuntu 20.04 / Debian 11. (From the library's dependencies; not reproduced.) Illegal instruction on x86_64 The CPU has no AVX2. Not verified: no such CPU was available. The host aborts when it exits runtime_cleanup() was not called. Changing num_threads has no effect 2.0.0 reads perf_mode, num_intra_threads and num_replicas instead.

docs.title: DEEPX
docs.text: 📦 Implementation details You can find the implementation of the DEEPX NPUs runtime & toolchain in the Github repository. This page describes its latest release, v2.0.0.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Accelerator DEEPX NPUs DX-M1 and DX-H1 (PCIe / M.2 cards) Engine DX-RT 3.3.2, one runtime build per Ubuntu version and CPU architecture Model format .dxnn, produced by the DEEPX compiler DX-COM 2.3.0 Toolchain image oaax-deepx-toolchain:2.0.0, 6.1 GB, x86_64 only, takes a .zip bundle Runtime library libRuntimeLibrary.so (about 180 KB), Ubuntu 20.04 / 22.04 / 24.04, x86_64 and aarch64 Runtime input one uint8 NHWC tensor, normalization is compiled into the model Not supported Windows, several models in one process Start here the end-to-end example: uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain deepx (6.1 GB image), then about 5 minutes of conversion

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
DEEPX NPUs are edge inference accelerators; DX-H1 is the higher-performance variant of the DX-M1.

  • Toolchain: converts an ONNX model to DXNN with DX-COM, which is installed in the Docker image (DEEPX permits redistributing it there). It quantizes the model with a calibration image set.
  • Runtime: implements the OAAX 2.0 interface on top of DX-RT. Inference is asynchronous and results come back in any order, matched by Tensors.id.
  • Model constraints (observed with DX-COM 2.3.0):
    • Single-input models. A two-input model fails with The dataloader provides a single input, but the model expects 2 inputs.
    • Static input shapes, declared in the JSON configuration.
    • The compiled model takes uint8 NHWC input. Only div / normalize preprocessing is compiled into it; resize, color conversion, crop and transpose are used for calibration only, so the host application must do them.
    • Operators the NPU does not run were placed in a CPU group instead of being rejected (tested with Erf, Einsum, CumSum).
    • Detection models keep their raw output heads: the host decodes boxes and applies NMS.
  • Does not do: image pre-processing, post-processing, float or layout conversion of the input.

DX-H1

DX-COM 2.3.0 reports Target Hardware: M1. DX-H1 conversion is not verified yet.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
• A DX-M1 or DX-H1 card (the DX-M1 is an M.2 Key M module, PCIe Gen3 x4 recommended) and its driver. Needed to run only.
  • Host CPU x86_64 or aarch64. Conversion needs an x86_64 host (the image is x86_64 only).

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
To run a model To convert a model OS Ubuntu 20.04, 22.04 or 24.04, the one the runtime was built for any Linux with Docker on x86_64 DEEPX software DX-RT 3.3.2, NPU driver, firmware none (DX-COM is in the image) Other a host application that calls the OAAX API; on a minimal image libgomp1 Docker, uv (for oaax-manager), 6.1 GB of disk for the image Network no no: converting works with --network none (tested); only downloading the image needs it

The DX-RT version must match exactly

The runtime links DX-RT dynamically and was built against 3.3.2. An older DX-RT fails to load it (see Troubleshooting).

Check what is installed:

dxrt-cli --status                        # first line: DXRT v<version>; also lists the driver, firmware and device
ldd libRuntimeLibrary.so | grep dxrt     # which libdxrt.so the runtime resolves

DX-RT is built from source (./install.sh --all && ./build.sh in the DX-RT repository, as the runtime's Docker build does); follow the DEEPX instructions for the driver and firmware. Windows is not supported yet: the Windows build job is disabled because the DX-RT Windows SDK repository is not reachable from CI.

docs.title: Get the runtime and toolchain
docs.text:
With oaax-manager, which verifies the checksums:

uvx oaax-manager list        # all builds; * = matches this CPU architecture (all three Ubuntu variants get a star: pick yours)
This machineAnother CPU (e.g. an aarch64 board)

uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime deepx --arch aarch64 --variant ubuntu22.04-dxrt3.3.2
