docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The input is a .zip with, at its root, exactly one .onnx, exactly one .json configuration and optionally a calibration image folder.

docker load -i oaax-deepx-toolchain-2.0.0.tar     # loads oaax-deepx-toolchain:2.0.0 and :latest
docker run --rm --user $(id -u):$(id -g) -v "$PWD:/work" oaax-deepx-toolchain:2.0.0 /work/model.zip /work/output

Output in ./output: <onnx name>.dxnn and convert.log (the toolchain writes no logs.json). Without --user the files belong to root. The official YOLOX-s with 100 calibration images took 4 min 42 s on a 20-core machine (see the example below).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The entrypoint takes only the two paths and reads no environment variable. Everything else goes in the JSON file:

JSON key Meaning inputs Required. {"<input name>": [N, C, H, W]}; must match the ONNX input names and shapes, else Input names mismatch / Input shape mismatch default_loader.dataset_path Calibration image folder, relative to the zip root (./calibration_dataset) default_loader.file_extensions Image extensions to use, e.g. ["jpeg", "jpg", "png"]; none found gives DataNotFoundError default_loader.preprocessings Ordered list applied to each calibration image, below calibration_num Number of calibration images used (100 in the DEEPX model zoo); more is slower calibration_method "ema" in all DEEPX examples. Other values are not validated by 2.3.0 ("foo" was accepted), see the DEEPX documentation train_batchsize, num_samples Present in the model-zoo YOLO configs, see the DEEPX documentation

Without default_loader the compiler warns No Data Loader is specified. Use Dummy Dataloader and still compiles, but the quantization is not calibrated on real data and accuracy may drop.

Preprocessing steps: resize (width+height, or mode, size, pad_location, pad_value, interpolation), convertColor (form, e.g. BGR2RGB), centercrop (width, height), div (x), normalize (mean, std), transpose (axis), expandDim (axis). An unknown step fails with Preprocessing transform '<name>' not found (sub does not exist). The log line Added nodes: Div(...) lists what was compiled into the model, Skipped nodes what the host must do. DEEPX's model zoo has ready-made configurations.

Advanced: DX-COM flags (bypass the entrypoint)

The entrypoint does not forward flags. To use them, run dxcom directly (tested with --opt_level 0 --gen_log):

docker run --rm --user $(id -u):$(id -g) -v "$PWD/w:/work" -w /work --entrypoint dxcom oaax-deepx-toolchain:2.0.0 \
  -m model.onnx -c model.json -o out --opt_level 0 --gen_log
Flag Effect --opt_level {0,1} default 1: faster NPU model, longer compile; 0: the opposite --aggressive_partitioning run as many operations as possible on the NPU --compile_input_nodes, --compile_output_nodes comma-separated node names to compile from / up to --float64_calibration float64 calibration, deterministic across CPUs --gen_log also write compiler.log and error.log to the output folder

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Message Cause Usage: ... <zip file> <output dir> not exactly two arguments Expected exactly 1 ONNX file, but found N / ... JSON file ... wrong count, or the files are in a sub-folder of the zip, or the zip path is wrong Error: dxcom conversion failed. followed by DX-COM's own error, e.g. ConfigFileError: You Must define input shapes, ConfigInputError, DataNotFoundError, DataPreprocessingError, DataLoaderError

Limits: the toolchain writes convert.log instead of logs.json, invalid config keys and calibration_method values are accepted silently, only a zip bundle is accepted, and the image is large (6.1 GB).

docs.title: Runtime library
docs.text: The runtime implements the OAAX 2.0 interface (runtime_get_name() returns DEEPX, runtime_get_version() 2.0.0).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
runtime_init reads no Config key: pass length = 0 (other keys are only logged at debug level). Settings are environment variables:

Variable Default Effect DEEPX_RUNTIME_LOG_FILE runtime.log log file (truncated at each runtime_init); logs also go to stderr SPDLOG_LEVEL info log verbosity (trace, debug, info, warn, error, critical, off) DXRT_DYNAMIC_CPU_THREAD ON (set by the runtime unless already set) DX-RT thread pool for the model's CPU parts; OFF is respected

ModelConfig: only file_path (the .dxnn file) is used. model_data, model_size and config are ignored, so a model cannot be loaded from memory.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• One model per process: runtime_load_models needs num_models == 1 and refuses a second model.
  • Input: only the first tensor is read. Its data_size must equal the model's input size; name, type and shape are not checked, so send uint8 NHWC.
  • Output: one tensor per model output, in the type and shape DX-RT reports (UNDEFINED for any type other than the 8 to 64-bit integers and float32). The caller frees it.
  • Concurrency: enqueue and retrieve can run on different threads. Results are unordered, so match them by Tensors.id. timeout_ms: 0 polls, positive waits, negative waits forever.
  • Backpressure: the output pool holds DX-RT's in-flight limit times the number of devices. When full, runtime_enqueue_input returns RUNTIME_STATUS_TIMEOUT at once: retry or drop the frame.
  • runtime_get_info() returns JSON: loaded_models, requests_in_flight, output_queue, pool_in_use, pool_size, pool_capacity. runtime_cleanup() waits for in-flight requests.
Status When NOT_INITIALIZED / ALREADY_INITIALIZED call before runtime_init / second runtime_init INVALID_ARGUMENT num_models != 1, a model is already loaded, null file_path FILE_NOT_FOUND the .dxnn file cannot be opened INVALID_MODEL DX-RT rejects the file (Failed to load model: ...) MODEL_NOT_LOADED, INVALID_MODEL_ID enqueue with no model / a model_id other than 0 INVALID_TENSOR no input tensor TENSOR_SHAPE_MISMATCH input size differs from the model's TIMEOUT output pool exhausted (backpressure) INFERENCE_ERROR DX-RT RunAsync failed; the caller keeps the input NO_OUTPUT_AVAILABLE retrieve timed out OUT_OF_MEMORY the output tensors could not be built

docs.title: End-to-end example
docs.text:
This converts the official YOLOX-s detector and runs it with the YOLOX example, one small C host that runs on every OAAX runtime; for DEEPX only two flags differ.

What step 6 needs

A DEEPX card, DX-RT 3.3.2, the driver and the firmware.

Before you start

Step 3 downloads the 6.1 GB toolchain image and step 4 takes about 5 minutes (4 min 42 s here, including the calibration download).

  1. Install the tools (Ubuntu), plus uv and Docker: 
    sudo apt-get install -y git curl cmake build-essential zip unzip libgomp1
  2. Get the example, build the host and download the model (the sha256 is checked): 
    git clone https://github.com/OAAX-standard/examples.git
cd examples/yolox-example
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build
bash fetch_model.sh
  3. Fetch the runtime and the toolchain, load the image: 
    . /etc/os-release
uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime deepx --variant ubuntu$VERSION_ID-dxrt3.3.2
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain deepx
docker load -i oaax-deepx-toolchain-2.0.0.tar
  4. Convert. The bundle holds the model, configs/deepx.json and 100 calibration images from DEEPX: 
    mkdir -p deepx/calibration_dataset
curl -fsSL https://sdk.deepx.ai/dataset/calibration_dataset.tar.gz | tar xz --strip-components=1 -C deepx/calibration_dataset
cp models/yolox_s.onnx deepx/ && cp configs/deepx.json deepx/yolox_s.json
(cd deepx && zip -qr yolox_s.zip yolox_s.onnx yolox_s.json calibration_dataset)
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/deepx:/work" oaax-deepx-toolchain:2.0.0 /work/yolox_s.zip /work/out
    It ends with Conversion finished at ... and deepx/out/yolox_s.dxnn exists.
  5. Check that the host and the runtime are in place: ls build/yolox_host runtime-deepx-*/libRuntimeLibrary.so.
  6. Run on the card. Check dxrt-cli --status (DX-RT 3.3.2), then run the host with the DEEPX flags (--layout nhwc --dtype uint8, the converted model takes raw uint8 NHWC pixels):
Same machineConvert on x86_64, run on an aarch64 board 
./build/yolox_host runtime-deepx-*/libRuntimeLibrary.so deepx/out/yolox_s.dxnn artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg \
  --layout nhwc --dtype uint8

Fetch the runtime on the board (uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime deepx --variant ubuntu$VERSION_ID-dxrt3.3.2), build the host there (steps 1 and 2), copy deepx/out/yolox_s.dxnn to it and run the same command.

The host prints the runtime name (DEEPX), the model's output tensor, the detections and OK: 10 requests ..., and writes detections.png. Output on a DX-M1 (DX-RT 3.3.2, Ubuntu 24.04):

Runtime: DEEPX 2.0.0
Input: 'images' uint8 NHWC, 1280x854 image letterboxed to 640
Output tensor 'output': type 1, shape [1, 8400, 85]
Detections (score >= 0.30, NMS IoU 0.45): 2
  bicycle        0.949  ( 613,  210) - (1228,  804)
  dog            0.927  ( 212,  247) - ( 521,  587)
Wrote detections.png
OK: 10 requests, first 34.6 ms (warm-up), then 24.3 ms on average (min 22.7 ms)

The same two objects as on the CPU runtime; boxes are within 4 px and scores within 0.01 because the model is quantized to INT8. Times depend on the host.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix undefined symbol: _ZN4dxrt14GetTaskMaxLoadEv or symbol lookup error when loading or calling the runtime The installed DX-RT is older than 3.3.2 (reproduced with 2.0.3). Install 3.3.2, run ldconfig, check with ldd libdxrt.so: cannot open shared object file DX-RT is not installed or not on the library path (it installs to /usr/local/lib, run ldconfig) GLIBC_... / GLIBCXX_... not found Wrong build for the OS: take the variant matching your Ubuntu (. /etc/os-release; echo $VERSION_ID) Device not found from dxrt-cli (also [DXRT][Error] Device not found., possibly followed by an abort), while lspci lists the card The driver is not loaded: lsmod | grep dx is empty and /dev/dxrt0 is missing. The driver is built for one kernel, so a kernel update removes it. In dx_rt_npu_linux_driver/modules run ./build.sh (needs linux-headers-$(uname -r)), sudo ./build.sh -c uninstall, sudo ./build.sh -c install --reload, then check dxrt-cli --status. If lspci does not list the card either, reseat it FILE_NOT_FOUND, Model file not found: <path> Wrong path to the .dxnn INVALID_MODEL, Failed to load model: ... The file is not a DXNN that this DX-RT accepts (an .onnx, truncated, or built by a very different DX-COM) TENSOR_SHAPE_MISMATCH, Input size X does not match model input size Y The host sent the wrong tensor, typically float or NCHW. Send uint8 NHWC of exactly Y bytes TIMEOUT from runtime_enqueue_input Too many requests in flight: retrieve outputs, then retry Multiple models not yet supported / Model already loaded One model per process: run several processes Conversion: DataLoaderError ... expects 2 inputs Multi-input models are not supported: export a single-input model Conversion: Input names mismatch inputs in the JSON does not use the ONNX input names Conversion: Expected exactly 1 ONNX file, but found 0 The files must be at the zip root, not in a folder Detections are wrong or empty The host's preprocessing does not match the preprocessings list (RGB order, resize, letterbox)

docs.title: ❓ OAAX Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
docs.text: Welcome to the OAAX FAQ. Below are answers to common questions about the OAAX standard, its goals, usage, and community.

docs.title: 🧠 General
docs.text:
What is OAAX? OAAX (Open AI Accelerator eXchange) is an open standard for deploying AI models across heterogeneous hardware (aka. XPUs) using a unified conversion and runtime interface. It enables portability, reproducibility, and modularity for AI model execution at the edge and beyond.

Why was OAAX created? AI hardware is fragmented — each vendor provides custom SDKs, runtimes, and conversion tools. OAAX addresses this fragmentation by standardizing the toolchain and runtime interface, making it easier to adopt new hardware or switch vendors without rewriting code.

Who is behind OAAX? OAAX is a project under the LF AI & Data Foundation. It is developed and maintained by a community of AI hardware vendors, software developers, and platform builders. The initial proposal was led by Network Optix.

What does OAAX stand for? Open AI Accelerator eXchange.

docs.title: 🔧 Usage
docs.text:
How do I use OAAX in my project?

  1. Convert your ONNX model using the OAAX Toolchain Docker image.
  2. Load the resulting OAAX bundle using the OAAX Runtime API.
  3. Enqueue inputs and retrieve outputs through a standardized C API.

See the Getting Started guide for full details.

What model formats are supported? Currently, OAAX supports ONNX format as input for model conversion. The output is a binary archive specific to the selected AI hardware.

Is OAAX only for inference? Yes. OAAX currently targets inference workloads only. Training workloads are out of scope.

docs.title: 💡 Technical Details
docs.text:
How does the runtime interface work? OAAX defines a minimal C API: runtime_init, runtime_load_models, runtime_enqueue_input, runtime_retrieve_output and runtime_cleanup, plus getters for the error, version, name and runtime info. Each hardware vendor implements this API to allow their device to run OAAX-converted models. See the specification.

Can one runtime run several models? Yes. runtime_load_models takes an array of models (from files or from memory), and each one is addressed by its index (model_id) when enqueuing inputs and retrieving outputs.

How do I match an output to its input? Set a unique id on each input Tensors. The runtime copies it onto the corresponding output.

Is the toolchain containerized? Yes. The conversion toolchain is packaged as a Docker image to isolate dependencies and ensure reproducibility. This also abstracts away vendor-specific conversion scripts.

Can I run multiple OAAX runtimes together? Yes. Each runtime is a separate shared library with the same interface, so an application can load several of them — each targeting a different accelerator — and drive each one through its own runtime_init ... runtime_cleanup lifecycle. A runtime is not stateless: it must be initialized before use and cleaned up afterwards.

What platforms does OAAX support?

  • Host OS: Linux (Ubuntu), Windows (limited)
  • Accelerators: CPU, Intel, NVIDIA, Hailo, DEEPX, and more in progress.
  • Languages: C/C++ (runtime), Python bindings coming soon

Does OAAX support dynamic batching or streaming? The API is asynchronous: inputs are enqueued without blocking and outputs are retrieved separately, so several requests can be in flight. Support for batching is vendor-specific. The standard itself allows for single or batched inputs; runtime implementations may offer optimizations.

docs.title: 📦 Contributions
docs.text:
How do I add support for a new accelerator? Vendors can contribute:

  • A toolchain Docker image that consumes ONNX and produces a valid bundle that can be loaded by the OAAX runtime.
  • A runtime implementation of the OAAX C API See the Contributing Guide for instructions.

Can I propose changes to the OAAX spec? Yes. OAAX is an open standard and encourages discussion via GitHub issues, pull requests, and mailing lists. Major changes go through the steering committee for review.

Where is the source code? All repositories are on the OAAX GitHub organization.

docs.title: 🧪 Compatibility
docs.text:
Is OAAX compatible with OpenVINO, TensorRT, or other toolkits? Yes, OAAX can act as a wrapper around vendor toolkits. For example, the Intel OAAX runtime internally calls OpenVINO. The goal is to standardize the outer interface while allowing flexibility inside.

Does OAAX guarantee performance parity with native SDKs? OAAX introduces a thin wrapper layer. While it may add negligible overhead, the performance largely matches native execution — assuming the vendor has optimized their runtime properly.

docs.title: 🔐 IP and Deployment
docs.text:
Can I keep my model private when using OAAX? Yes. OAAX as a standard allows keeping models private. It's up to the vendor's implementation to handle model compilation (by the toolchain) and loading (by the runtime) securely.

Is the runtime sandboxed? No, the runtime runs natively. However, you can deploy it inside containers, isolated services, or with limited permissions.

docs.title: 📣 Community
docs.text:
How do I get help?

  • GitHub Discussions: OAAX-standard/OAAX
  • Slack: Coming soon

How often does the standard change? OAAX aims for stable, versioned releases. Breaking changes are minimized to maintain compatibility.

docs.title: 🧾 Licensing & Legal
docs.text:
What license is OAAX released under? OAAX is licensed under the Apache 2.0 License, encouraging open contribution and commercial use.

Have a question that isn't answered here? 💬 Open a GitHub Issue to help us improve this FAQ.

docs.title: Hello World Example
docs.text:
This walkthrough takes the official YOLOX object detector through the two OAAX stages and prints what it finds in a photo:

  1. Convert the ONNX model with the chip's conversion toolchain (a Docker image).
  2. Run the converted model with the chip's runtime library, through one small C host application.

The host is the same for every chip: only the runtime library and the converted model change. That is the point of OAAX.

The picture the host writes. Photo: Dog from Barcelona 01.jpg by Nicolas Vigier, CC0 1.0.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A Linux x86_64 machine (Ubuntu 22.04 or higher) with Docker that your user can run without sudo.
  • uv, which runs the OAAX tools: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh, then export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH".
  • Build tools: sudo apt-get install -y git curl cmake build-essential libgomp1 ca-certificates zip (zip is needed for the Intel, DEEPX and Hailo tabs).
  • The hardware of the chip you pick, with its driver on the machine that runs the model: for Intel GPU or NPU the Intel drivers (see the Intel page; the CPU device needs none), for NVIDIA a driver and the CUDA 13 libraries, for DEEPX a card with DX-RT 3.3.2, for Hailo a Hailo-8 with HailoRT 4.20.0.

docs.title: 1. Build the host and get the model
docs.text:
The YOLOX example is a C program that loads any OAAX 2.0 runtime, runs the model on an image, prints the detections and draws them. It has no dependencies besides a C compiler and CMake.

git clone https://github.com/OAAX-standard/examples.git
cd examples/yolox-example
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build
bash fetch_model.sh                          # writes models/yolox_s.onnx (36 MB, sha256 checked)

docs.title: 2. Convert and run
docs.text:
CPUIntelNVIDIADEEPXHailo

Downloads 844 MB (toolchain 835 MB, runtime 8.5 MB).

uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime cpu
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain cpu
docker load -i oaax-cpu-toolchain-2.0.0.tar

mkdir -p model && cp models/yolox_s.onnx model/
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/model:/model" oaax-cpu-toolchain:2.0.0 /model/yolox_s.onnx /model/output

./build/yolox_host runtime-cpu-2.0.0-linux-x86_64/libRuntimeLibrary.so model/output/yolox_s-simplified.onnx artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg

More on the CPU toolchain and runtime: CPU page.

Downloads 1.3 GB (toolchain 1.2 GB, runtime 90 MB). The config keeps the model's float32 input; by default the Intel toolchain converts to FP16 and the runtime then expects FP16 tensors.

uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime intel
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain intel
docker load -i oaax-intel-toolchain-2.0.0.tar

mkdir -p intel/input intel/output && cp models/yolox_s.onnx intel/input/model.onnx && cp configs/intel.json intel/input/config.json
(cd intel/input && zip model.zip model.onnx config.json)
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/intel/input:/input" -v "$PWD/intel/output:/output" oaax-intel-toolchain:latest /input/model.zip /output

./build/yolox_host runtime-intel-2.0.0-linux-x86_64/libRuntimeLibrary.so intel/output/model.zip artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg

When the container runs as your own user (--user $(id -u):$(id -g)), the conversion prints harmless OpenVINO telemetry warnings. The runtime uses the CPU device by default: add --config device_type=GPU (or NPU) to use that device, and check effective_device in the Runtime info line, because a device that cannot run the model falls back to the CPU. More: Intel page.

Downloads 1.8 GB (toolchain 967 MB, runtime 823 MB). This is the ONNX Runtime build: the conversion needs no GPU, and the run needs an NVIDIA driver for CUDA 13 and the CUDA 13 libraries (libcudart, libcublas, libcublasLt, libcufft).

uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime nvidia-ort --variant cuda13
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain nvidia-ort
docker load -i oaax-nvidia-onnxruntime-toolchain-2.0.0.tar

mkdir -p ort && cp models/yolox_s.onnx ort/model.onnx
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/ort:/model" oaax-nvidia-toolchain:2.0.0 /model/model.onnx /model/output

./build/yolox_host runtime-nvidia-ort-2.0.0-linux-x86_64-cuda13/libRuntimeLibrary.so ort/output/model-simplified.onnx artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg

On an RTX A4000 this takes about 11 ms per request. TensorRT, the faster NVIDIA runtime, and the other CUDA versions: NVIDIA page.

Downloads 6.1 GB (toolchain 6.1 GB, runtime 180 KB) and 100 calibration images from DEEPX. The conversion takes about 5 minutes on any x86_64 machine; running the model needs a DEEPX card with DX-RT 3.3.2 and its driver, so copy deepx/out/yolox_s.dxnn and the runtime there if that is another machine. The converted model takes raw uint8 NHWC pixels, hence the two flags.

. /etc/os-release
uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime deepx --variant ubuntu$VERSION_ID-dxrt3.3.2
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain deepx
docker load -i oaax-deepx-toolchain-2.0.0.tar

mkdir -p deepx/calibration_dataset
curl -fsSL https://sdk.deepx.ai/dataset/calibration_dataset.tar.gz | tar xz --strip-components=1 -C deepx/calibration_dataset
cp models/yolox_s.onnx deepx/ && cp configs/deepx.json deepx/yolox_s.json
(cd deepx && zip -qr yolox_s.zip yolox_s.onnx yolox_s.json calibration_dataset)
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/deepx:/work" oaax-deepx-toolchain:2.0.0 /work/yolox_s.zip /work/out

./build/yolox_host runtime-deepx-*/libRuntimeLibrary.so deepx/out/yolox_s.dxnn artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg --layout nhwc --dtype uint8

On a DX-M1 this takes about 24 ms per request. More: DEEPX page.

Downloads 1.2 GB (toolchain 1.2 GB, runtime 8 MB). Converting needs Hailo's own SDK, which is not redistributable: the Dataflow Compiler wheel, the HailoRT wheel and the HailoRT .deb, in a hailo-deps/ folder (see the Hailo page). The conversion takes about 14 minutes; running the model needs a Hailo-8 with HailoRT 4.20.0.

uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime hailo --variant hailort4.20.0
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain hailo
docker load -i oaax-hailo-toolchain-2.0.0.tar

mkdir -p hailo/input hailo/output && cp models/yolox_s.onnx hailo/input/ && cp configs/hailo.json hailo/input/yolox_s.json
(cd hailo/input && zip yolox_s.zip yolox_s.onnx yolox_s.json)
docker run --rm -e PIP_FIND_LINKS=https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/jax_releases.html \
  -v "$PWD/hailo-deps:/app/hailo-deps" -v "$PWD/hailo/input:/app/input:ro" -v "$PWD/hailo/output:/app/output" \
  onnx-to-hailo:latest /app/input/yolox_s.zip /app/output
sudo chown -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" hailo/output      # the container writes as root

./build/yolox_host runtime-hailo-2.0.0-linux-x86_64-hailort4.20.0/libRuntimeLibrary.so hailo/output/yolox_s.hailo8.onnx artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg --input-name input0

The SDK renames the model's input to input0, hence the flag. On a Hailo-8 this takes about 12 ms per request. More: Hailo page.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
On the CPU (the other chips print their own runtime name and Runtime info line, and the same two detections; the INT8 models of DEEPX and Hailo move the boxes by a few pixels):

Runtime: OAAX CPU Runtime 2.0.0
Runtime info: {"loaded_models":1,"requests_in_flight":0,"backend_version":"1.17.3"}
Input: 'images' float32 NCHW, 1280x854 image letterboxed to 640
Output tensor 'output': type 1, shape [1, 8400, 85]
Detections (score >= 0.30, NMS IoU 0.45): 2
  bicycle        0.953  ( 616,  210) - (1228,  806)
  dog            0.934  ( 216,  244) - ( 521,  587)
Wrote detections.png
OK: 10 requests, first 90.5 ms (warm-up), then 91.4 ms on average (min 71.9 ms)

detections.png is the picture above. Timings depend on your machine. The program exits with a non-zero code if a request fails, and the runtime writes runtime.log in the current directory.

Other chips and builds

NVIDIA TensorRT (the fastest NVIDIA runtime), other CUDA, HailoRT and Ubuntu versions, Windows and Arm builds are on the accelerator pages: CPU, Intel, NVIDIA, Hailo, DEEPX. The example's README has the commands for every chip.

docs.title: Download and check with the OAAX tools
docs.text:
Two small command-line tools, run with uv (the tools themselves need no install):

  • oaax-manager (GitHub) downloads a runtime or toolchain for your machine and verifies its checksum:
uvx oaax-manager list                    # what is available (* = matches this machine)
uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime cpu       # writes runtime-cpu-2.0.0-linux-x86_64/libRuntimeLibrary.so
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain cpu     # saves oaax-cpu-toolchain-2.0.0.tar and prints the `docker load` command

The example above already uses it; the same two commands exist for every chip (intel, nvidia-ort, nvidia-trt, hailo, deepx).

  • oaax-conformance (GitHub) checks a runtime or toolchain against the specification:
uvx --python 3.12 --from 'oaax-conformance[e2e]' oaax-conformance runtime ./libRuntimeLibrary.so --model @tiny-conv --out report
uvx --python 3.12 --from 'oaax-conformance[e2e]' oaax-conformance toolchain oaax-cpu-toolchain:2.0.0 --out report

Open report/report.html for the details. Exit code 0 means every required check passed. The reference CPU runtime and toolchain have known findings, so exit code 1 is expected for them.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read how the host talks to a runtime: the YOLOX example README, the smaller c-example and the runtime specification.
  • Use your own model: export it to ONNX (for example yolo export model=yolov8n.pt format=onnx with Ultralytics, which is AGPL-3.0: check the license before redistributing a model or an application built on it), convert it with the toolchain, and adapt the pre- and post-processing in the host application.
  • Add your own accelerator: see the specification and the reference implementation.

docs.title: Hailo
docs.text: 📦 Implementation details You can find the implementation of the Hailo runtime & toolchain in the Github repository. This page describes the latest release (v2.0.0).

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Start here Check your HailoRT version (how), then follow the end-to-end example. NPU class Dedicated AI accelerator on a PCIe / M.2 module Chips Hailo-8 HailoRT versions 4.17.0, 4.18.0, 4.19.0, 4.20.0: one runtime build per version Engine ONNX Runtime with the Hailo execution provider, on top of HailoRT Model format ONNX in, <model>.hailo8.onnx out (the compiled model is wrapped in an ONNX file) Runtime library libRuntimeLibrary.so (Ubuntu, x86_64 and aarch64) Toolchain image onnx-to-hailo:latest (Docker, x86_64 hosts only, 1.2 GB, needs Hailo's SDK files) How far it is verified Run on a Hailo-8 with HailoRT 4.20.0. The 4.17 to 4.19 runtimes are only compiled and symbol-checked by CI. Hailo-8L is not verified.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Toolchain: unpacks a zip (ONNX model, an options JSON, optional calibration images) and runs the Hailo SDK steps parse, optimize (INT8 quantization with the calibration images) and compile for the hailo8 architecture. It writes <model>.hailo8.onnx: a graph whose HailoOp node embeds the compiled model, followed by the parts of the original graph the chip cannot run.
  • Runtime: loads that file with ONNX Runtime; the Hailo execution provider runs the HailoOp node on the chip through HailoRT and everything else on the host CPU. Inputs and outputs keep the types and layout of the converted graph (float32 NCHW in and out for YOLOX and YOLOv8).
  • One runtime build per HailoRT version: each archive bundles its own libhailort, which must match the HailoRT driver installed on the host.
  • Model constraints: the Hailo SDK decides which operators convert; the repository does not list them. It documents YOLOv8n, YOLOv8s and YOLOX-s as converting, and YOLO11n and YOLO26n as failing (attention layers, SDK 3.25.0). The model needs one image input with a fixed size.
  • Not done: no Hailo-8L target, no model script or optimization level, no batch or device selection, no accuracy check, no decoding of detections (the host does it).

Limits

A wrong input name, an unconverted model and a failed conversion do not fail loudly (see Troubleshooting). The toolchain compiles for hailo8 only.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
• A Hailo-8 module (PCIe or M.2) in an x86_64 or aarch64 host.
  • Conversion needs an x86_64 Linux machine (the image and Hailo's compiler are x86_64 only). Copy the converted model to an aarch64 device afterwards.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
Needed to Requirement Run Ubuntu 20.04 or higher (the libraries need glibc 2.29 and libstdc++ from GCC 9; Ubuntu 22.04 was used for this page) libatomic1 and libgomp1: sudo apt-get install libatomic1 libgomp1 Hailo's PCIe driver (hailort-pcie-driver) installed, with /dev/hailo* present A runtime build whose HailoRT version equals the installed driver version (below) Convert Docker, and internet access (the container installs the SDK's Python dependencies at every start) From Hailo's Developer Zone (login required, not redistributable): hailo_dataflow_compiler-3.<minor>.0-py3-none-linux_x86_64.whl, hailort-4.<minor>.0-cp310-cp310-linux_x86_64.whl and the matching hailort_4.<minor>.0_amd64.deb (it provides libhailort, which the wheel needs; an empty or placeholder file is not enough), one version of each in one folder

The image holds Ubuntu 22.04 and Python 3.10 (hence cp310). The example below was converted with Dataflow Compiler 3.29.0 and the HailoRT 4.19.0 wheel; which compiler goes with which HailoRT is not documented. A model converted that way runs on the 4.20.0 runtime.

Pick the runtime variant: it is the version of the installed driver.

hailortcli --version                 # HailoRT-CLI version 4.20.0
dpkg -l | grep -i hailo              # hailort and hailort-pcie-driver, same version
modinfo hailo_pci | grep ^version    # driver version
hailortcli scan                      # lists the devices

docs.title: Get the runtime and toolchain
docs.text:
oaax-manager (0.1.1 or newer, which fixed the Hailo checksums; check with uvx oaax-manager --version) downloads and verifies both. Install uv first.

uvx oaax-manager list                                                         # Hailo rows: hailort4.17.0 ... hailort4.20.0
uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime hailo --variant hailort4.20.0                  # -> runtime-hailo-2.0.0-linux-x86_64-hailort4.20.0/
uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime hailo --variant hailort4.20.0 --arch aarch64   # for an aarch64 device
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain hailo                                        # -> oaax-hailo-toolchain-2.0.0.tar

--variant is required (several builds exist). The runtime folder holds libRuntimeLibrary.so, libonnxruntime_providers_hailo.so, libonnxruntime_providers_shared.so, libhailort.so.<version> and oaax_runtime.h. Keep them together: the companion libraries are found next to libRuntimeLibrary.so.

docs.title: Download links and compatibility matrix
docs.text: Runtime libraries are packaged as library-<HailoRT version>.tar.gz (same files as above). SHA-256 sums are in the release notes; sizes are in brackets.

docs.title: OAAX 2.0
docs.text:
Conversion toolchain (any platform with Docker): Download (1.2 GB)

OS CPU architecture HailoRT Runtime library Ubuntu x86_64 4.17.0 Download (8 MB) Ubuntu x86_64 4.18.0 Download (8 MB) Ubuntu x86_64 4.19.0 Download (8 MB) Ubuntu x86_64 4.20.0 Download (8 MB) Ubuntu aarch64 4.17.0 Download (7 MB) Ubuntu aarch64 4.18.0 Download (7 MB) Ubuntu aarch64 4.19.0 Download (8 MB) Ubuntu aarch64 4.20.0 Download (8 MB)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
1. Put the three SDK files in hailo-deps/ and make a zip with the model and an options JSON (below). Without calibration images the toolchain uses the 100 COCO images it ships with (the SDK used 64 of them in the YOLOX run).
  2. Load the image. Its name and tag come from the tar: onnx-to-hailo:latest (no versioned tag).
  3. Run it. Do not pass --user: the container installs the SDK as root and fails otherwise. Pass -e PIP_FIND_LINKS=https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/jax_releases.html with Dataflow Compiler 3.29: it requires jaxlib==0.4.13, which is gone from PyPI.
docker load -i oaax-hailo-toolchain-2.0.0.tar
docker run --rm -e PIP_FIND_LINKS=https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/jax_releases.html \
  -v "$PWD/hailo-deps:/app/hailo-deps" -v "$PWD/input:/app/input:ro" -v "$PWD/output:/app/output" \
  onnx-to-hailo:latest /app/input/model.zip /app/output
sudo chown -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" output     # the container wrote as root

The entry point takes exactly two arguments (zip path, output folder, both inside the container). Every start re-installs the SDK; the conversion itself took about 14 minutes for YOLOX-s.

docs.title: Zip contents
docs.text: File Rule *.onnx Exactly one, at the top level. Its name decides the output name. *.json Exactly one, at the top level: the options below. *.jpg, *.jpeg Optional calibration images, anywhere in the zip. Resized (stretched) to width x height.

docs.title: Options JSON
docs.text:
Key Type Default Meaning height, width int required Model input size; calibration images are resized to it. channels int required 1 = grayscale calibration images, anything else = RGB. nchw bool required Layout of the calibration array. Keep false: Hailo expects NHWC data whatever the model's layout. means, stds list of numbers required Calibration pixels become (pixel - mean) / std (pixels are 0 to 255). Give the runtime the same normalization. One value or one per channel. start_node_names list of strings [] Where the SDK starts parsing; empty = the model's inputs. end_node_names list of strings [] Where the SDK stops parsing; the nodes after stay plain ONNX on the host. Empty = auto-detect the YOLOv8 head (finds only 6 of the 9 head nodes of YOLOX, so list them); other models: the whole graph.

Other keys are ignored. The YOLOX-s file of the example (configs/hailo.json in the examples repository):

{"start_node_names": [],
 "end_node_names": ["Sigmoid_264", "Conv_261", "Sigmoid_263", "Sigmoid_285", "Conv_282", "Sigmoid_284", "Sigmoid_306", "Conv_303", "Sigmoid_305"],
 "height": 640, "width": 640, "channels": 3, "nchw": false, "means": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], "stds": [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]}

docs.title: Outputs, logs and errors
docs.text:
The output folder gets <model>.hailo8.onnx and logs.json (and possibly a tmp/ folder: the unzipped input). logs.json is a list of {"Message": ..., "Data": {...}}:

Message Data Converting ONNX to Hailo-ONNX Input Path Starting conversion Target Hardware (hailo8); stages Translation, Optimizing Model, Compiling Model set to Done as they finish Auto-detected end nodes nodes: the cut found for YOLOv8 models Successful Conversion (last) MIME type (application/x-onnx; device=hailo-8), Output Path Conversion Failed (last) Human Error (always the same generic text), Technical Error (the real reason)

The exit code is 0 even when the conversion fails

Check that the last message is Successful Conversion. Only the failures before the conversion below give a non-zero exit code.

Message Meaning and fix dpkg: error: cannot access archive '../hailo-deps/hailort_4.*.0_amd64.deb' (exit 2) hailo-deps not mounted, or the file is missing or misnamed. dpkg: error: requested operation requires superuser privilege (exit 2) You passed --user. Remove it. Usage: /app/scripts/convert.sh <onnx-path> <output-directory> (exit 1) Wrong number of arguments. Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement jaxlib==0.4.13 Add PIP_FIND_LINKS (above). Technical Error No module named 'hailo_sdk_client' The SDK wheels were not installed; read the container's log above. Technical Error The HailoRT Python API (hailo_platform package) must be installed After a 14-minute compile: the HailoRT wheel is there but its libhailort (from the .deb) is not. Install the real .deb of the same version. Technical Error File is not a zip file, No ONNX file found in the zip, More than one ONNX file found in the zip (same for JSON) Fix the zip. Technical Error 'means' (or another key) A required options key is missing. Technical Error from the SDK parser (may recommend other end nodes) An operator is not supported. Use the recommended end_node_names / start_node_names, or another model.

The compiler warns that with fewer than 1024 calibration images and no GPU it lowers the optimization level; this is why INT8 boxes can differ by about 10 pixels from the CPU run. Give it more images if that matters.

docs.title: Runtime library
docs.text: The library implements the OAAX runtime interface. Unknown config keys are ignored.

docs.title: runtime_init keys
docs.text:
Key Values Default Meaning log_level 0 debug, 1 info, 2 warning, 3 error 1 Minimum level written to the log file. Out of range = 1; a non-numeric value counts as 0. log_file path runtime.log Base name: the files are <log_file>.0, .1, ... (a new one every 4 MiB, appended to). The console always gets INFO and above. n_threads 1 to 16 4 ONNX Runtime threads in total, split evenly over all replicas of all models (at least 1 each). Above 16 = 16; 0, negative or non-numeric = ignored (perf_mode applies). perf_mode eco, power unset Only used when n_threads is not set: 40% (eco) or 90% (power) of the online cores, at least 1. Another value = 4. n_replicas 1 or more 1 ONNX Runtime sessions, each with its own worker thread, per model. Below 1 = 1.

The threads only run the ONNX nodes that stay on the CPU (for YOLOX: slicing in front, reshapes behind); the chip works inside HailoRT. There is no device-selection key. HailoRT writes its own hailort.log in the working directory.

docs.title: Models and inputs
docs.text:
• ModelConfig: give file_path (or model_data + model_size). ModelConfig.config is unused. At most 8 models; a model's id is its index in the array. Models load once per runtime_init.
  • Inputs are bound by tensor name, in any order. The name must be the one in the converted model: the SDK renames the input to input0, so read it from the .hailo8.onnx file (onnx.load(path).graph.input), not from your original model.
  • Each model has an input queue and the runtime one output queue, 100 items each. When full, the oldest item is dropped and runtime_enqueue_input still succeeds: keep retrieving. With several replicas outputs can come back in any order: match them by Tensors.id.
  • Enqueueing and retrieving can be done from different threads. To switch models, call runtime_cleanup and runtime_init again. The library exports only the OAAX API (checked in CI), so a host can unload it and load another copy.

docs.title: Status codes and errors
docs.text:
Call Status When runtime_init ALREADY_INITIALIZED (3) Called twice without runtime_cleanup. runtime_load_models NOT_INITIALIZED (2), ALREADY_INITIALIZED (3), INVALID_ARGUMENT (5) No init; models already loaded; fewer than 1 or more than 8 models. ERROR (1) Any model failure (missing file, unsupported model, chip unreachable, version mismatch). runtime_get_error() says Failed to create ORT session for replica N; the reason is in the log (ORT error: ...). runtime_enqueue_input NOT_INITIALIZED (2), MODEL_NOT_LOADED (4), INVALID_MODEL_ID (18), INVALID_ARGUMENT (5) Wrong call order, bad id, NULL tensors. runtime_retrieve_output NO_OUTPUT_AVAILABLE (12) Nothing within the timeout (0 = do not wait, negative = wait forever).

A bad input is not reported to the caller

A wrong tensor name, type or shape is accepted by runtime_enqueue_input. The request fails in the worker, is logged (Inference run failed and the ONNX Runtime reason) and no output arrives: the host sees NO_OUTPUT_AVAILABLE.

runtime_get_info() returns {"loaded_models":N,"requests_in_flight":N,"backend_version":"..."}. If the log file cannot be opened the library exits the process: use a writable log_file.

docs.title: End-to-end example
docs.text:
Goal: the official YOLOX-s model (Apache-2.0) from ONNX to detections on a Hailo-8, with the YOLOX example of the examples repository as host. The same host runs every OAAX chip; for Hailo only the model and one flag change.

Before you start

Step 4, the conversion, needs Hailo's SDK, which is not redistributable: it takes about 14 minutes (Dataflow Compiler 3.29.0, HailoRT 4.19.0 wheel). Step 5 runs on a Hailo-8 with HailoRT 4.20.0.

Prerequisites: a Linux x86_64 machine with the Hailo-8 driver and uv; sudo apt-get install git curl cmake build-essential libgomp1 zip and Docker; and the three SDK files in hailo-deps/ (Software).

  1. Build the host and get the model (the model's sha256 is checked):

    git clone https://github.com/OAAX-standard/examples.git && cd examples/yolox-example
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build
bash fetch_model.sh                       # models/yolox_s.onnx

  2. Get the runtime and the toolchain, with the variant equal to your HailoRT version:

    uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime hailo --variant hailort4.20.0
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain hailo && docker load -i oaax-hailo-toolchain-2.0.0.tar

  3. Pack the model with the options of the example:

    mkdir -p hailo/input hailo/output && cp models/yolox_s.onnx hailo/input/ && cp configs/hailo.json hailo/input/yolox_s.json
(cd hailo/input && zip yolox_s.zip yolox_s.onnx yolox_s.json)

  4. Convert (about 14 minutes; the container runs as root):

    docker run --rm -e PIP_FIND_LINKS=https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/jax_releases.html \
  -v "$PWD/hailo-deps:/app/hailo-deps" -v "$PWD/hailo/input:/app/input:ro" -v "$PWD/hailo/output:/app/output" \
  onnx-to-hailo:latest /app/input/yolox_s.zip /app/output
sudo chown -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" hailo/output

    The last message of hailo/output/logs.json must be Successful Conversion.

  5. Run the host with the converted model (input0 is the renamed input):

    ./build/yolox_host runtime-hailo-2.0.0-linux-x86_64-hailort4.20.0/libRuntimeLibrary.so hailo/output/yolox_s.hailo8.onnx \
  artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg --input-name input0

What you should see: Runtime: OAAX Hailo Runtime 2.0.0, an output tensor of shape [1, 8400, 85], two detections (bicycle and dog, scores 0.953 and 0.934) and OK: 10 requests, then detections.png, the picture with the boxes. The unconverted model on the CPU runtime gives the same classes and scores, with boxes within about 11 pixels (INT8). As an example, the Hailo-8 took about 12 ms per request and the CPU about 80 ms on the test machine; yours will differ.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Failed to create ORT session for replica 0; hailort.log says Driver version (4.20.0) is different from library version (4.19.0) (HAILO_INVALID_DRIVER_VERSION(76)) Runtime variant differs from the driver Download the variant equal to the driver version (how to check). Same, with HAILO_DRIVER_FAIL(36) / Failed to query driver info Same mismatch (seen with a 4.17.0 library on a 4.20.0 driver) Same fix. Same, hailortcli scan lists nothing, no /dev/hailo* Driver not installed or loaded Install hailort-pcie-driver, reload or reboot, check lsmod \| grep hailo and the permissions of /dev/hailo*. Requests accepted, no output, NO_OUTPUT_AVAILABLE; log has Invalid Feed Input Name:<name> Input name differs from the converted model's Use the name inside the .hailo8.onnx (input0 in the example). Unexpected input data type in the log Tensor type differs from the model's Send the types the converted model declares. Model loads, but it is slow and the chip is idle An unconverted ONNX was loaded: it runs on the CPU Load the .hailo8.onnx; it has a HailoOp node. libatomic.so.1 or libgomp.so.1: cannot open shared object file Missing system library sudo apt-get install libatomic1 libgomp1. MLDataType for: tensor(float) is not currently registered after switching runtimes A runtime build older than 2.0.0 Use the 2.0.0 builds. Conversion fails or exits strangely See Outputs, logs and errors Includes the jaxlib and missing-libhailort cases. Conversion: SDK parse error on a YOLO11 or other new model Operators the SDK version does not support Use a supported model or a newer SDK, or cut the graph with start_node_names / end_node_names.

docs.title: Intel
docs.text: 📦 Implementation details You can find the implementation of the Intel CPU, GPU and NPU runtime & toolchain in the Github repository, and its latest release in v2.0.0.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Devices Intel CPU, integrated or discrete GPU (Arc, Iris Xe, UHD, Data Center GPU) and NPU (Linux), one runtime for all three Engine OpenVINO™ 2026.1.0 (native C++ API) Toolchain input .zip bundle with model.onnx and an optional config.json (plus calibration images for INT8) Toolchain output <model>.zip with the OpenVINO IR (model.xml and model.bin), plus logs.json Toolchain image oaax-intel-toolchain:latest (Docker, x86_64, about 1.2 GB) Runtime library libRuntimeLibrary.so (Linux x86_64) or RuntimeLibrary.dll (Windows x86_64), shipped with the OpenVINO libraries Device choice device_type = CPU (default), GPU, NPU or AUTO, global or per model Start here uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime intel and uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain intel, then the end-to-end example

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The toolchain converts an ONNX model to OpenVINO IR. The runtime loads that IR and runs it on the Intel device you select.

  • Toolchain: by default it compresses the weights to FP16 and turns every model input into FP16. Optionally it quantizes to INT8 (NNCF) or bakes input conversion, mean and scale into the model. It does not change the model's operators or outputs.
  • Runtime: it loads one or more .zip IR bundles, runs requests asynchronously and returns outputs tagged with the request id. It accepts an input tensor only if its data type is exactly the IR input's type (no conversion), and any shape the IR allows (batch 1 by default, a fixed batch or a dynamic batch if you convert it so).
  • Devices: the runtime asks OpenVINO for the device; if compiling the model on a non-CPU device fails, it falls back to the CPU and says so only in runtime.log and in runtime_get_info (effective_device).

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Device Supported Intel hardware (OpenVINO system requirements) Checked by us CPU Core 6th to 14th gen and Core Ultra, Xeon, Atom. The runtime refuses to start without AVX2 Core i7-12700K GPU Arc, Iris Xe, UHD / HD Graphics, Data Center GPU Flex and Max UHD Graphics 770 (integrated) NPU Core Ultra NPU Verified on Linux. Not supported on Windows yet

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
To run a converted model:

Linux Windows OS Ubuntu 22.04 or higher, Debian 12 or higher (needs glibc 2.34 and libstdc++ 3.4.30) Windows 10, 11 (x86_64) (not verified) System packages libgomp1. Minimal images (containers) do not have it none, the Visual C++ runtime DLLs are in the archive OpenVINO included in the runtime archive (2026.1.0), nothing to install included GPU an OpenCL GPU driver, see Installation Intel graphics driver NPU the NPU driver, see Installation Not supported yet

To convert a model: Docker 20.10 or higher on an x86_64 host and 1.2 GB of disk for the image. Python, OpenVINO (2026.4.1 in the image, not pinned) and NNCF 2.19 are inside the image.

Tools for the steps of this page: uv (runs oaax-manager), zip, and to build the example host git, curl, cmake and build-essential. On a minimal image (container) install them all: sudo apt-get install -y git curl cmake build-essential zip libgomp1.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Only GPU and NPU need drivers. The CPU needs none.

GPU (Ubuntu)NPU (Ubuntu)Windows 
sudo apt-get install -y ocl-icd-libopencl1 intel-opencl-icd
sudo usermod -aG render $USER     # log out and in again

This is what we verified (Ubuntu 22.04, integrated GPU). For newer GPUs use Intel's current driver packages, see the OpenVINO GPU guide. Discrete Arc GPUs want kernel 6.2 or higher.

Install the driver from intel/linux-npu-driver; it needs Ubuntu 22.04 or higher with kernel 6.6 or higher. See the OpenVINO NPU guide.

Install the current Intel graphics driver (GPU), see the guide above. The NPU is not supported on Windows yet.

A GPU or NPU request can silently run on the CPU

If the device is missing or the model does not compile on it (no driver, no access to /dev/dri, user not in the render group, no --device /dev/dri in Docker), the run still succeeds, on the CPU. The reason is only in runtime.log. Always check effective_device in runtime_get_info() (the Runtime info: line of the example host) and available_devices for the devices OpenVINO found.

GPU means any OpenCL GPU

Without the Intel driver, a host with another vendor's OpenCL GPU lists that GPU as GPU, and the runtime uses it. With several GPUs, GPU becomes MULTI:GPU.0,GPU.1,...; use GPU.0, GPU.1 to pick one.

docs.title: Get the runtime and toolchain
docs.text:
With oaax-manager (needs uv); it verifies the sha256 of every download. The vendor is intel; there are no variants.

uvx oaax-manager list                    # the Intel rows: runtime linux, runtime windows, toolchain
uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime intel     # writes runtime-intel-2.0.0-linux-x86_64/ (all 31 files)
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain intel   # saves oaax-intel-toolchain-2.0.0.tar
docker load -i oaax-intel-toolchain-2.0.0.tar
uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime intel --os windows   # the Windows runtime

docs.title: Download links and compatibility matrix
docs.text:
Runtime libraries are packaged as library.tar.gz. Extract all the files into the same directory: the runtime finds the OpenVINO libraries next to itself, no LD_LIBRARY_PATH needed. The sha256 of each file is in the v2.0.0 release notes.

OAAX version OS Version CPU architecture Runtime library Conversion toolchain 2.0.0 Ubuntu 22.04 or higher x86_64 Download (90 MB) Download (1.2 GB) 2.0.0 Windows 10, 11 x86_64 Download (61 MB) ⬆️

docs.title: Conversion toolchain
docs.text:
The image has the tag oaax-intel-toolchain:latest only (there is no :2.0.0 tag; the version is in the image label version=2.0.0). Its entrypoint is conversion_toolchain INPUT_ZIP OUTPUT_DIR. The container runs as root by default, so pass your own user to own the output files:

mkdir -p input output
cp model.onnx input/ && (cd input && zip model.zip model.onnx)
docker run --rm --user $(id -u):$(id -g) -v "$PWD/input":/input -v "$PWD/output":/output \
  oaax-intel-toolchain:latest /input/model.zip /output

Bundle layout

model.onnx (any *.onnx name; if there are several, the first is used and a warning is logged) and config.json must be at the root of the zip, not in a folder. The output is named after the ONNX file: model.onnx gives model.zip.

docs.title: config.json options
docs.text:
Every key is optional. Unknown keys are ignored. Example: { "optimization": { "fp16_compression": false } }.

Key Type, default Effect optimization.fp16_compression bool, true Stores the weights in FP16 (half the size) and, unless preprocessing.input_dtype is set, makes every input FP16. false keeps the model's input types (for example FP32). Forced to false when quantizing optimization.quantization.enabled bool, false INT8 post-training quantization (NNCF). Needs calibration images; makes the input u8 with /255 baked in, whatever scale_values says optimization.quantization.preset mixed, performance, accuracy; mixed performance quantizes all layers (fastest). accuracy is accepted but gives the same IR as mixed optimization.quantization.subset_size int > 0, 300 Maximum number of calibration images used optimization.quantization.target_device any, cpu, gpu, npu; any NNCF target. npu forces performance and keeps attention and DFL MatMuls in FP16 optimization.quantization.mode, .calibration_data int8, "calibration/" Accepted, no effect: INT8 is always used, the folder is found by name (below) preprocessing.input_dtype u8, f16, f32 or null Element type of all inputs; the IR converts back to the model's type inside preprocessing.mean_values, .scale_values list of numbers or null (x - mean) / scale per channel, baked in and applied to every input (rank 4 is read as NCHW, rank 3 as CHW) advanced.batch_size int > 0, 1 Fixes the batch dimension. Fails if the model has batch 1 hard-coded in its post-processing advanced.dynamic_batch bool, false Makes the batch dimension dynamic (-1). Excludes batch_size > 1 model_file, advanced.input_shape, .input_names, .output_names Accepted, no effect

Input type of the converted model:

Config Input type in the IR default f16 fp16_compression: false unchanged (usually f32) quantization enabled u8 preprocessing.input_dtype set the value you set

INT8: add "quantization": {"enabled": true} under optimization and put JPEG, PNG, BMP or TIFF images in calibration/ (images/ or data/ also work) in the zip: zip -r model.zip model.onnx config.json calibration/. Images are resized to the model's height and width. Calibration assumes a single image input.

docs.title: Output and errors
docs.text:
<model>.zip holds model.xml and model.bin. logs.json is a JSON array of {Timestamp, Message, Data} steps; the last one is Successful Conversion (output name, MD5, optimizations applied) or FATAL ERROR: ... with the error. The log is also printed. Exit codes and the messages we triggered:

Exit Meaning Message seen 0 Success 1 Input not found Input zip file does not exist: /input/x.zip 2 Invalid input or config Invalid zip archive: File is not a zip file (a bare .onnx was passed); No ONNX model (*.onnx) found in input archive (model missing or in a folder); Invalid quantization preset: ...; Invalid batch_size: 0 ...; dynamic_batch=true and batch_size > 1 are mutually exclusive; Quantization is enabled but no calibration data provided ...; malformed JSON, e.g. Expecting ',' delimiter ... 3 Conversion or quantization failed OpenVINO error text. Example: INT8 on a model with a second, non-image input fails with Layout [...] doesn't have channels dimension, because the u8 and /255 step is applied to every input 4 I/O error (permissions, disk full) 255 Unexpected error

docs.title: Runtime library
docs.text: The runtime implements the OAAX runtime interface. runtime_init(Config) takes string key/value pairs; unknown keys are ignored with a warning in the log. Invalid values fall back to the default.

docs.title: runtime_init keys
docs.text: Key Values, default Meaning device_type CPU (default), GPU, NPU, AUTO, or any OpenVINO device name (GPU.1) Device used by the models. GPU with several GPUs becomes MULTI:GPU.0,GPU.1,.... AUTO starts on the CPU and moves to an accelerator when ready. A device that does not exist or fails to compile falls back to the CPU perf_hint latency (default), throughput, cumulative_throughput OpenVINO performance mode. Use cumulative_throughput with MULTI. Other values mean latency num_requests int, 0 = auto Parallel inference requests per model. Auto asks OpenVINO (we saw 1 with latency, 4 to 5 with throughput) num_streams int, 0 = auto OpenVINO streams, only used with throughput; 4 is recommended for a discrete GPU auto_batch_size int, 0 = off Wraps the device in BATCH:<device>(N) to batch concurrent requests. Ignored on the CPU npu_turbo 1 or 0 (default) Sets NPU_TURBO=YES on an NPU (Linux only) cache_dir path, . (default), "" = off OpenVINO compiled-model cache (<hash>.blob files), shared by all models. It avoids recompiling at every start and is created in the current directory by default max_queue_size int, 100, 0 = unlimited Pending inputs per model and pending outputs. When full, runtime_enqueue_input returns RUNTIME_STATUS_ERROR (input queue at capacity) log_level 0 trace to 6 off, 2 (default) Minimum log level log_file path, runtime.log Log file, rotated at 5 MB. Each start begins a fresh file and keeps the last three as runtime.1.log to runtime.3.log. If it cannot be opened, the runtime logs to the console log_stdout 1 or 0 (default) Also log to the console

docs.title: Per-model keys
docs.text: ModelConfig.config accepts device_type, perf_hint and num_requests, which override the global value for that model, for example to run a detector on the GPU and a classifier on the CPU. cache_dir is accepted there but has no effect: the cache directory is global. The other keys are global only.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Models: ModelConfig.file_path must be the .zip from the toolchain (a .onnx or .xml fails with Failed to extract model archive). It is unpacked into the temp directory (TMPDIR) and removed at cleanup. Load all models in one runtime_load_models call; a second call returns ALREADY_INITIALIZED until runtime_cleanup(). The model id is its index.
  • Data types: the input type must equal the IR's, otherwise runtime_enqueue_input returns RUNTIME_STATUS_INVALID_ARGUMENT with dtype mismatch for input 'x': model expects f16 but caller sent f32. Supported types: float, float16, bfloat16, double, int8 to int64, uint8 to uint64, bool, string, int4, uint4.
  • Output shapes: outputs have the IR's data type. An output with a dynamic dimension (for example the number of detections) has the exact size on the CPU, but on the GPU we saw it padded to its upper bound with zero rows.
  • Shapes: a wrong shape or an unknown input name is not reported by runtime_enqueue_input (see Troubleshooting).
  • Concurrency: each model has its own pool of inference requests and a queue; all outputs go to one queue, in completion order, so match them by Tensors.id. Enqueue and retrieve can be called from different threads. Keep at least num_requests inputs in flight to keep a fast model busy.
  • Diagnostics: runtime_get_info() returns JSON: loaded_models, requests_in_flight, output_queue_depth, backend_version, perf_hint, max_queue_size, available_devices and per model effective_device, num_infer_requests, input_queue_depth, inputs (name, dtype, shape, -1 = dynamic) and outputs.
  • Environment variables: none are required. OAAX_DEBUG_CORE_TYPE (ANY, PCORE, ECORE) forces the CPU core type; it is for diagnostics only.

You can check out the examples repository for more details on how to use the runtime library: OAAX Examples.

docs.title: End-to-end example
docs.text:
The generic YOLOX example (yolox_host, the official yolox_s.onnx, a CC0 test image): from nothing to detections. It takes about a minute on a fast connection.

Prerequisites

Docker and uv, then sudo apt-get install -y git curl cmake build-essential zip libgomp1. For the GPU or NPU tab, the drivers from Installation.

  1. Build the host and download the model (36 MB, sha256 checked):

    git clone https://github.com/OAAX-standard/examples.git
cd examples/yolox-example
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build
bash fetch_model.sh

  2. Download the runtime (90 MB) and the toolchain (1.2 GB) and load the image:

    uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime intel
uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain intel && docker load -i oaax-intel-toolchain-2.0.0.tar

  3. Convert the model. configs/intel.json is { "optimization": { "fp16_compression": false } }, which keeps the float32 input of the model (about 4 s):

    mkdir -p intel/input intel/output && cp models/yolox_s.onnx intel/input/model.onnx && cp configs/intel.json intel/input/config.json
(cd intel/input && zip model.zip model.onnx config.json)
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/intel/input:/input" -v "$PWD/intel/output:/output" oaax-intel-toolchain:latest /input/model.zip /output

    With --user and no home directory the toolchain prints a few openvino_telemetry warnings; they are harmless.

  4. Run it. --config device_type=... is passed to runtime_init:

    CPUGPUNPU 
    ./build/yolox_host runtime-intel-2.0.0-linux-x86_64/libRuntimeLibrary.so intel/output/model.zip artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg --config device_type=CPU

    ./build/yolox_host runtime-intel-2.0.0-linux-x86_64/libRuntimeLibrary.so intel/output/model.zip artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg --config device_type=GPU

    In Docker add --device /dev/dri and the render group. Check "effective_device":"GPU", see the warning in Installation.

    ./build/yolox_host runtime-intel-2.0.0-linux-x86_64/libRuntimeLibrary.so intel/output/model.zip artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg --config device_type=NPU

    Linux only: the NPU is not supported on Windows yet. Without an NPU the command still succeeds, with "effective_device":"CPU".

Output on the CPU (the Runtime info line is shortened; it is one long JSON line):

Runtime: OAAX Intel 2.0.0
Runtime info: {"loaded_models":1,...,"available_devices":["CPU","GPU"],"models":[{"id":0,"effective_device":"CPU",...
Input: 'images' float32 NCHW, 1280x854 image letterboxed to 640
Output tensor 'output': type 1, shape [1, 8400, 85]
Detections (score >= 0.30, NMS IoU 0.45): 2
  bicycle        0.953  ( 616,  210) - (1228,  806)
  dog            0.934  ( 216,  244) - ( 521,  587)
Wrote detections.png
OK: 10 requests, first 95.4 ms (warm-up), then 61.7 ms on average (min 46.8 ms)

detections.png shows the boxes. On the integrated GPU (effective_device GPU) we got the same two objects with identical boxes and scores (checked against the CPU run), and first 39.7 ms (warm-up), then 34.2 ms on average. Times depend on the machine.

Default (FP16) conversion: send float16

Without config.json the toolchain makes the input float16. Pass --dtype float16 to the host:

mkdir -p intel16/input intel16/output && cp models/yolox_s.onnx intel16/input/model.onnx
(cd intel16/input && zip model.zip model.onnx)
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/intel16/input:/input" -v "$PWD/intel16/output:/output" oaax-intel-toolchain:latest /input/model.zip /output
./build/yolox_host runtime-intel-2.0.0-linux-x86_64/libRuntimeLibrary.so intel16/output/model.zip artifacts/dog-bicycle.jpg --config device_type=CPU --dtype float16

The result is the same two objects (59.5 ms on average here). Without the flag the host stops with dtype mismatch for input 'images': model expects f16 but caller sent f32.

INT8: YOLOX finds nothing (known behavior)

The toolchain bakes a /255 into every INT8 model and ignores scale_values, but YOLOX expects raw 0-255 pixels. A yolox_s converted with "quantization": {"enabled": true} (calibration images in calibration/) and run with --dtype uint8 finds no detections. Workaround (untested): add a Mul by 255 after the input of the ONNX before converting.

docs.text: 📦 Implementation details The runtime and toolchain are implemented in the nvidia-acceleration repository. Latest release: v2.0.0.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Devices NVIDIA GPUs (TensorRT toolchain: compute capability 7.5 or higher), Jetson, DGX Spark / Grace Backends ONNX Runtime with the CUDA Execution Provider (nvidia-ort), native TensorRT 10 or 11 (nvidia-trt) Runtime library libRuntimeLibrary.so (Linux), RuntimeLibrary.dll (Windows, ONNX Runtime only), 1 MB to 1.7 GB depending on the build Toolchain image oaax-nvidia-toolchain:2.0.0 (967 MB) or oaax-nvidia-tensorrt-toolchain:2.0.0 (11 GB) Start here uvx oaax-manager fetch runtime nvidia-ort --variant cuda13 and uvx oaax-manager fetch toolchain nvidia-ort, then the end-to-end example Verified / not Verified on an RTX A4000, driver 580, CUDA 13, Ubuntu x86_64: both backends (ONNX Runtime and TensorRT 10), with the YOLOX example. Not verified: Windows, Jetson, DGX Spark / Grace (SBSA), TensorRT 11 conversion, running the CUDA 11 package, the wheel conversion path, docker run --gpus all as written Which backend and --variant? Backend --variant (Linux x86_64; other platforms) The simplest path, any model, Windows, or to convert without a GPU ONNX Runtime (nvidia-ort) cuda13, or the CUDA major you have installed (cuda11, cuda12; check with ldconfig -p \| grep libcublasLt) The fastest inference, a model with fixed-size outputs TensorRT (nvidia-trt) ubuntu22.04-trt10-cuda13 (TensorRT 10 matches the Docker toolchain)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
NVIDIA GPUs are supported through two backends that expose the same OAAX 2.0 runtime interface, so the host application does not change. Use the runtime and the toolchain of the same backend together.

ONNX Runtime backend TensorRT backend Platforms Linux x86_64, Jetson, SBSA, Windows x86_64 Linux x86_64, Jetson, SBSA (same GPU classes) Toolchain input .onnx file (no GPU needed) .zip bundle: model.onnx + config.json (needs the target GPU) Toolchain output model-simplified.onnx model.trt engine, built for the GPU it ran on Runtime accepts .onnx path or in-memory buffer; bundles ONNX Runtime and cuDNN .trt path or in-memory buffer; bundles TensorRT and libcudart
  • ONNX Runtime (start here): the toolchain only simplifies the graph, so you can convert on any machine, and the runtime executes the model with the CUDA Execution Provider. Broadest model coverage and the only backend on Windows.
  • TensorRT: the toolchain compiles an engine for the exact GPU in the machine (trtexec), and the runtime loads it directly. Best inference performance, but the engine only runs on the GPU architecture, CPU platform and TensorRT version it was built for.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Item Requirement GPU An NVIDIA GPU. The TensorRT toolchain refuses GPUs below compute capability 7.5 (Turing). Verified on an RTX A4000 (8.6). Both runtimes always use GPU 0: pick another with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. GPU memory Depends on the model. ORT: the CUDA memory arena grows on demand (cap it with gpu_mem_limit). TRT: the engine plus one set of input/output buffers per concurrent slot (max_concurrent). Jetson / DGX Spark, Grace (sbsa) Jetson, ORT: JetPack 5 (CUDA 11), 6 (CUDA 12) or 7 (CUDA 13); TRT: JetPack 6 only (CUDA 12, TensorRT 10). SBSA, ORT: CUDA 13; TRT: Ubuntu 24.04, TensorRT 10 (CUDA 12 or 13) or TensorRT 11 (CUDA 13).

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
Needed to run (runtime) Needed to convert (toolchain) Tools libgomp1 (needed by both runtimes). docker; TRT also zip. To fetch and try the example: uv, git, curl, cmake and build-essential (minimal images lack them: sudo apt-get install -y git curl cmake build-essential libgomp1 zip). OS Linux: Ubuntu 20.04+ for CUDA 11/12 ORT builds; Ubuntu 22.04+ for the CUDA 13 ORT builds and all TRT builds (glibc 2.29 / 2.34 / 2.33). Windows 10/11 (ORT only). Docker on any Linux x86_64 host (ORT). Docker plus the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, or the Python wheel with a local TensorRT (TRT). NVIDIA driver New enough for the package's CUDA major version, per NVIDIA's compatibility table: CUDA 11 needs 450.80+, CUDA 12 needs 525.60+, CUDA 13 needs 580+. TRT only: a driver for CUDA 13 (580+), with nvidia-smi working on the host. CUDA libraries ORT: not bundled. Install the CUDA major of your package: libcudart, libcublas, libcublasLt and libcufft (Windows: on PATH). TRT: bundled (libcudart and TensorRT), nothing to install. None on the host (they are inside the image). cuDNN ORT: bundled, except on Jetson (JetPack provides it) and for the cuda12 x86_64 package (see the warning below). TRT: not used. None TensorRT TRT: bundled (10.16 or 11.0); an engine only loads in a runtime with the same TensorRT version as the toolchain that built it. Jetson: not bundled, JetPack provides it. The image contains TensorRT 10.16, so use a trt10 runtime with it. The TRT 11 runtime needs the wheel with TensorRT 11 installed.

Known issue: the cuda12 ONNX Runtime package (Linux x86_64) needs cuDNN 8

The 2.0.0 cuda12 package contains cuDNN 9 files, but its ONNX Runtime (1.16.3) loads cuDNN 8 (libcudnn.so.8), so it fails with libcudnn.so.8: cannot open shared object file. Download cuDNN 8.9.7.29 for CUDA 12 from NVIDIA and place it next to libRuntimeLibrary.so (about 786 MB of libraries):

curl -fLO https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cudnn/redist/cudnn/linux-x86_64/cudnn-linux-x86_64-8.9.7.29_cuda12-archive.tar.xz
tar xJf cudnn-linux-x86_64-8.9.7.29_cuda12-archive.tar.xz --wildcards "*/lib/libcudnn.so.8*" "*/lib/libcudnn_*_infer.so.8*"
cp -P cudnn-linux-x86_64-8.9.7.29_cuda12-archive/lib/libcudnn.so.8* cudnn-linux-x86_64-8.9.7.29_cuda12-archive/lib/libcudnn_*_infer.so.8* runtime-nvidia-ort-2.0.0-linux-x86_64-cuda12/

(sha256 of the archive, 865 MB: 475333625c7e42a7af3ca0b2f7506a106e30c93b1aa0081cd9c13efb6e21e3bb.) No LD_LIBRARY_PATH is needed for cuDNN, because the runtime libraries look in their own folder. The cuda11 and cuda13 packages are not affected: they bundle the cuDNN version they load (8.9.7 and 9.25). The CUDA 12 libraries (libcudart, libcublas, libcufft) must still be installed on the host.
